items.headline: 中情局長密訪莫斯科
items.context: 美國媒體報導，中情局局長瑞特克里夫（Ratcliffe）搭乘美軍飛機，經拉脫維亞飛往俄羅斯，進行未公開的會談。克里姆林宮否認與美方有相關會談。

items.context: 美國賓夕法尼亞州兩名未接種疫苗的人死於麻疹。美國今年的麻疹病例數，來到病毒被視為根除以來的新高，專家警告，疫苗接種率下滑，讓這個原本幾乎絕跡的疾病重新找到破口。

items.context: 美國法官駁回吉思蓮・麥斯威爾（Ghislaine Maxwell）推翻定罪的聲請，認定她的主張「毫無根據」。她原本希望新公開的艾普斯坦（Jeffrey Epstein）檔案，能幫助她推翻性販運相關罪名。

sources.summary: As a child, being taken to the Caribbean celebration was a drag. But once sound systems arrived in the 1970s, it became an unmissable yearly pilgrimage offering a sense of freedom My earliest memories of the Notting Hill carnival are of being mildly irritated. In its 1960s infancy, the event was strictly a Caribbean affair, transplanted to Ladbroke Grove as authentically as was practical. Its purpose was as obvious as its origins: giving Caribbean arrivals a chance to celebrate themselves by bringing the vibrancy of the home they left behind to these drab streets for a couple of days. Vital as this was – and it really was – it didn’t cut much ice with surly 10- or 11-year-olds like me, being dragged around behind parading steelbands. Yes, it was great to see so many Black people out in the open together and your mums and dads laughing and having a good time, but did we need to be here? There was football to be played and bikes to be ridden, yet so many of us were being forced to walk for what seemed like miles following “old people music”. Continue reading...

sources.summary: Yang has taken more than 500,000 photographs since he first moved to Sydney in the late 1960s and now devotes most of his time to untangling the past As a young adult, William Yang discovered that his family’s story was actually a murder mystery. His uncle, William Fang Yuen, was killed by an employee on the family’s farm in far north Queensland in 1922, but his mother refused to tell him the full story. In 1990, he travelled to Innisfail in search of the truth. One aunt told Yang that his uncle and the worker had got into a fight over a gambling debt, and the worker had stabbed him to death with a spear. A cousin said a gang was involved. A local woman, who had been a child at the time, remembered it as a card game gone wrong. Continue reading...

sources.summary: Soprano with razor-sharp articulation who created lead roles including the Duchess of Argyll in Powder Her Face A lustrous vocal quality, combined with an alluring, exuberant stage presence, ensured the popularity of the soprano Jill Gomez, who has died aged 83, on both operatic stage and concert platform. When her talent came to the fore in the early 1970s she was hailed by Arthur Jacobs in Opera magazine, along with Josephine Barstow, as “the most exciting of our newer female singers”, while reviews of the time hailed her Governess in Britten’s The Turn of the Screw and Anne Trulove in Stravinsky’s The Rake’s Progress as among the finest. The latter role was one of those she took, along with Mélisande, Calisto and Helena (A Midsummer Night’s Dream), at Glyndebourne, where Gomez enjoyed her first major successes, appearing between 1969 and 1984. At Covent Garden her roles included Lisa in La Sonnambula, Titania in A Midsummer Night’s Dream and Lauretta in Puccini’s Gianni Schicchi. Continue reading...

items.context: 衛報本輪評論橫跨舞台劇、電影與書籍。愛丁堡藝穗節喜劇《The Librarians》嘲諷職場崩壞，致敬經典情境喜劇；動作片《Zip Wire》講一名患強迫症的抗癌科學家，被迫吊在鋼索上對抗殺手；詩人克勞蒂亞・蘭金（Claudia Rankine）新書《Triage》探討面對世界殘酷時該如何自處；娜塔莎・華特（Natasha Walter）新作《Feminism for a World on Fire》則把氣候危機與全球正義運動連在一起。

items.threads_text: 這輪衛報評論橫跨舞台劇、電影與書籍，四篇題材差很多。愛丁堡藝穗節喜劇《The Librarians》裡，一間搖搖欲墜的圖書館館長猝逝，接手的新館長一邊處理突擊檢查、一邊面對電線老舊、來客銳減的窘境，被拿來和經典職場喜劇《辦公室風雲》相提並論。動作驚悚片《Zip Wire》則有點荒謬——女主角是治好了肺癌的科學家，患有嚴重強迫症，卻被迫吊掛在義大利多洛米蒂山區一條老舊鋼索上，一邊對抗殺手一邊維持理智。書籍這邊，美國詩人克勞蒂亞・蘭金新作《Triage》，用回憶錄、小說與批評交織，探討面對戰爭與氣候危機這類集體創傷時，人該如何自處；娜塔莎・華特的《Feminism for a World on Fire》，則把氣候危機和全球正義運動放在一起討論，被形容是在絕望中帶來希望的作品。
items.voice_text: 這次的藝文評論，橫跨舞台劇、電影跟書。先講喜劇。愛丁堡藝穗節有一齣《The Librarians》，講一間搖搖欲墜的圖書館，館長突然過世，新館長一邊要應付突擊檢查，一邊要面對電線老舊、沒什麼人來的窘境，被拿來跟經典職場喜劇比。換個調性，看電影。《Zip Wire》有點荒謬，女主角是剛治好肺癌的科學家，還有嚴重強迫症，結果被迫吊在山區的鋼索上跟殺手周旋。最後看書。詩人克勞蒂亞・蘭金新書談的是，面對戰爭跟氣候危機這種集體創傷，人該怎麼自處；另一本《Feminism for a World on Fire》，把氣候危機和全球正義運動擺在一起看，評論說這本書在絕望裡，找到了一點希望。

sources.summary: Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh Well-tuned performances help along a familiar set of laughs as a rickety library gets a new manager and an inspection The sign says Plumstanton Library but this could be The Brittas Empire’s Whitbury New Town Leisure Centre, The Office’s Wernham Hogg or Torquay fleapit Fawlty Towers. Such is the instant familiarity of a failing workplace whose staff have a new manager and an inspector to contend with at once. It’s not only the books that are well worn in Matthew Howell and Jack Michael Stacey’s play. Acting head librarian Harry Wordsworth has even bought his own “best boss” mug like David Brent. Nevertheless it’s a frequently funny hour, with well-tuned performances. Harry (Matthew Howell) finds himself in charge when Peter, who has run the library for more than 25 years, pops his clogs in the Agatha Christie section. This death in the aisle is both a tragedy and mystery which the remaining staff stumble through, beset by dodgy electrics, dwindling visitors and a seemingly inevitable closure. sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: This nonsensical film sees an OCD-afflicted scientist fending off assassins while hanging from an aerial wire, and fails to get pulses racing for even a minute In this silly, low-adrenaline thriller, the title star is a rickety old zip wire bolted into the side of a mountain in the Italian Dolomites that was never intended for human use. It was constructed in the first world war to sling weapons and supplies hundreds of feet down the valley – and is still used to get the occasional goat off the mountain. But for the second half of this film, a world-famous British research scientist with an extreme fear of heights dangles from it, fighting off highly skilled assassins in increasingly preposterous ways. The scientist is Amy (MyAnna Buring); she has discovered a cure for lung cancer, and her drive is explained in syrupy hospital-ward flashbacks to her mother dying when she was a teenager. Amy also has OCD – she is so anxious about germs that she never takes off her rubber gloves, and has an assistant in her lab to do anything that involves touching or handling objects. (Like all the characters, she never gets beyond a stereotype.) Her research is bankrolled by a big pharma company, whose CEO is played by Saffron Burrows (now seemingly mandatory casting for ropey British thrillers). Continue reading...

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: The American poet and essayist weaves memoir, fiction, criticism and lyrical lament into a tale of friendship in an age of existential crisis “Any resemblance to actual persons, living or dead, or actual events is purely coincidental,” writes the multi-award winning Jamaican-American poet, essayist and playwright Claudia Rankine in the disclaimer to her latest work. “Unless it isn’t.” The pretzel-logic of this statement, its assertive ambiguity, sets the tone for a book that digs directly into the question of what we are to do with the idea of truth, when the world we live in is asking us “to hold, visually and emotionally, realities we do not yet have a viable system of language for”. In Triage, Rankine borrows from her personal history and from a world whose landscape now encompasses “the rise of fascism, the implementation through deportations of the Great Replacement theory, the starvation of devastated populations subjected to war and climate change”, and uses the material she gathers to pose a simple question. When faced with realities such as these, what do you do? Do you stand, or do you fall? The book begins with a friendship. Two young people – our narrator, and another she refers to only as “the theorist” – meet in college in the late 20th century, and are drawn to each other. They’re passionate; they’re idealistic; they’re committed to the activism of the time (“shantytowns were built on campus to protest apartheid South Africa”) and steeped in the texts and authors and philosophical conceits of the humanities. Over time, they develop a game. “When we spied each other during the day,” the narrator explains, “we had to collapse.” Continue reading...

sources.summary: A writer and activist links the climate crisis to battles for justice around the world in this vital book It has become increasingly difficult to change our minds, to question our own views or to find common ground with people we disagree with, all of which makes Natasha Walter’s new book both refreshing and exhilarating. In her ebullient 1998 debut The New Feminism, Walter hailed Margaret Thatcher as a trailblazer. In this fiercer, bleaker work, she rips into the “glossy language of aspiration feminism”, “the message that the individual woman can do anything she wants if she only has the necessary courage”. That kind of feminism inspired an “explosion of books and films about pioneers and heroines, about bossy women and gutsy girls” which retold the feminist story as “a succession of isolated campaigns, led by outsize individuals”. sources.summary: Underbelly, Edinburgh Maddie and Marcus Rice relate with words and songs the lessons passed on from one woman to a younger one An unexpected theme on this year’s Edinburgh fringe is assisted dying. It is central to Morna Young’s After Party , about a matriarch who chooses to die after her 80th birthday, and Ben Harrison’s adaptation of Andrew O’Hagan’s Mayflies , in which a terminally ill man travels to Dignitas. It is hinted at in Eilidh Loan’s Cathy , about a woman adjusting to bereavement. And it is here again in this breezy storytelling show by sibling duo Maddie and Marcus Rice. The semi-fictional tale is about Maddie’s befriending of the 87-year-old Darcy O’Shea, an artist and piano teacher 50 years her senior, who is full of zest and vigour. As Maddie puts it, she is “unapologetically herself”, a woman living a life of happy self-reliance with limited tolerance for anyone else. A long-gone partner nicknamed her Dandelion because of her sticky-up hair, and it suits her personality. At Underbelly, Edinburgh, until 30 August All our Edinburgh reviews Continue reading...

sources.summary: The oberek is a traditional dance beloved of state folk ensembles – but a new generation of musicians is reconfiguring its music into wild new forms, merging folk steps with electronics and the sound of Chicago footwork It’s 6pm on the first day of OFF festival in Katowice, and a crowd is gathering in front of one of the stages to watch newcomers Tercet Imperial. Sporting disco outfits of nylon jackets, tracksuits and Chicago Bulls caps, keyboardist Piotr Zabrodzki deploys resonant acid melodies, while drummer Jan Emil Młynarski plays a rapid, irregular rhythm that brings to mind the scattergun beats of footwork, the ghetto-house subgenre that grew out of Chicago in the late 90s. Not many of those jerking their limbs to the music in front of the stage are likely to realise that they are listening to a distinctly Polish sound: that of the oberek, a traditional dance in triple metre whose name derives from the Polish verb “to spin”, because it usually accompanies couples whirling across dancefloors in a circular motion. sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: A brilliant new biography that does it subject the favour of taking her seriously – even if few else did Barbara Cartland was famous for dictating her novels. With a pekingese clamped to her hot pink bosom she would lie back on a library couch and exhale a story about virginal girls taming wayward dukes, damaged airmen or misunderstood surgeons. Meanwhile Miss Savory, Mrs Smith or Mrs Morgan, picked for being unfidgety and sneezeless, would take everything down in immaculate Pitman shorthand. Cartland reckoned on being able to polish off 8,000 words a day. “In this way,” she told one of the many reporters who quizzed her on her astonishing productivity, “the typescript for an 80,000-word novel is finished in a fortnight.” At her peak she was pushing out 23 books a year which added up to 723 in total. Only Agatha Christie and William Shakespeare topped her lifetime sales of 750m. Cartland was a dictator in other ways, too. Husbands, dogs, houses and the local council were all expected to bend themselves to her indomitable will. Resistance, let alone opposition, was futile. The managing director of the company that printed her books suggested that she read Nietzsche on the perceptive grounds that they had a lot of ideas in common. Oddly, he also declared himself madly in love with her. Behind that marshmallowy exterior, all pink chiffon, candyfloss hair and soft, smudgy lines, there lurked sinews of high-tensile steel. Continue reading...

items.context: 美國對加拿大課徵50%關稅，讓不少加拿大企業幾乎無法再賣進美國市場，經濟學家示警恐衝擊大量就業機會。加拿大隨後宣布對美系列產品課徵「一美元對一美元」的報復性關稅，範圍涵蓋化妝品、乳製品、木材與戶外用品等產業。

items.headline: 澎湖漁業科僅1新生
items.context: 澎湖縣唯一的高職，今年漁業相關科系新生人數幾乎腰斬，其中漁業科更只有1名新生入學。退休教師陳明宗憂心，澎湖漁業將出現勞動力斷層。
items.thread_text: 澎湖縣唯一的高職，今年漁業相關科系新生人數幾乎腰斬，漁業科甚至只有1名新生入學。退休教師陳明宗擔心，這會讓澎湖漁業出現勞動力斷層。縣府農漁局副局長陳銓汶回應，將持續透過補助等方式，鼓勵青年投入漁業，並培育遠洋漁業觀察員等專業人才。
